title: The Pet Cemetery Murders: The Real Case Behind HBO's Ghost Story

lines.say: In April 1985, the woman who ran a pet cemetery in south Louisiana disappeared.

shots.label: ILLUSTRATION · GENERIC PET CEMETERY, NOT THE REAL SITE

lines.say: She was due in court within days, in a lawsuit over her land.
Less than a month later, fishermen found her in the Mississippi River, weighted down with steel chains.
The sheriff said police had a prime suspect from the very start: her own groundskeeper.

shots.label: ILLUSTRATION · GENERIC PET CEMETERY, NOT THE REAL SITE

lines.say: But there was no physical evidence. No arrest. And the case went cold.

shots.label: ILLUSTRATION · GENERIC PET CEMETERY, NOT THE REAL SITE

lines.say: In 2009, a man went to the police. He said the groundskeeper had confessed to him.
And he said something else. Her ghost was haunting his dreams.
Three years later, a prison inmate came forward. He said he was there when she was killed.
The case rested almost entirely on that one witness. And in 2014, the groundskeeper pleaded guilty. Not to murder. To manslaughter.
This is the real case behind HBO's The Pet Cemetery Murders. What the record shows, and what it doesn't.

shots.kicker: THE REAL CASE · ST. BERNARD PARISH, 1985

lines.say: Dorothy Thompson was sixty-one.
She owned the Azalea Original Pet Cemetery, out in Toca, in rural eastern St. Bernard Parish.

shots.label: ILLUSTRATION · GENERIC PET CEMETERY, NOT THE REAL SITE

lines.say: Her mother, Grace, had opened it around 1950.

shots.label: ILLUSTRATION · GENERIC PET CEMETERY, NOT THE REAL SITE

lines.say: And at the centre of this story is her land: fourteen acres in Toca.

shots.label: Toca, St. Bernard Parish
shots.note: The land at the centre of the dispute

lines.say: Brandon Nodier worked at the cemetery, as its groundskeeper and handyman.

shots.label: ILLUSTRATION · GENERIC PET CEMETERY, NOT THE REAL SITE

lines.say: According to investigators, he tricked her into signing her land over to him.
Dorothy said she'd been tricked, and she sued to get it back.

rows.text: She sued to get it back

lines.say: The case was heading for a courtroom in Chalmette.
In mid-April 1985, just days before that court date, Dorothy Thompson disappeared.
She was last seen at a bank in eastern St. Bernard.

shots.label: ILLUSTRATION · GENERIC ROAD, EASTERN ST. BERNARD

lower.title: Last seen
lower.kicker: A bank in eastern St. Bernard

lines.say: The Sheriff's Office later said it believed she was suffocated, inside her own home, on the thirteenth of April.
On the second of May, fishermen found her body in the Mississippi River, on the east bank of Plaquemines Parish.
She had been weighted down with steel chains.
From the start, the sheriff said, Brandon Nodier was the prime suspect.
Investigators said he wanted her land. But there was no physical evidence tying him to her death, and not enough to arrest anyone.

shots.label: ILLUSTRATION · GENERIC DETECTIVE, NOT A LIKENESS

lines.say: In the early years, State Police detectives were so stumped, they brought in a psychic from Slidell.
It didn't lead to an arrest. And for years, the case went cold.

shots.label: ILLUSTRATION · GENERIC PET CEMETERY, NOT THE REAL SITE

lines.say: Then Hurricane Katrina hit, and the Sheriff's Office lost its files.
But one State Police file survived. It would help rebuild the case.
In 2009, Detective John Doran, of the St. Bernard Parish Sheriff's Office, reopened the case.
Doran said a man had come forward, and told police that Nodier had confessed to him.
And then, according to Doran, the man said something stranger. Dorothy's ghost, he said, was haunting his dreams.
It still wasn't enough to charge anyone.
Then, in 2012, according to police, a man serving time in prison got in touch.
He said he'd been Nodier's assistant groundskeeper. And he said he was there when Dorothy Thompson was killed.
Police didn't name him. He was given immunity from prosecution, in exchange for his account.
So why did he come forward, after all that time?
He said Dorothy's ghost had started haunting him, too.
But The Advocate, in New Orleans, reported a more down-to-earth reason. It said he went to the authorities only after Nodier visited him in jail, and threatened him and his wife.
Two witnesses, and two ghost stories. But only one of them said he saw what happened.
In April 2012, a St. Bernard Parish grand jury indicted Brandon Nodier, then fifty-eight, for second-degree murder.
He turned himself in, and was freed on bond.
It had taken twenty-seven years.

shots.label: 1985 to 2012
shots.note: From her death to the arrest

lines.say: The case never went to a jury.
In 2014, under a plea deal, Nodier pleaded guilty. Not to murder, but to manslaughter.
He was sixty. He was sentenced to ten years in prison.
Judge Perry Nicosia accepted the plea. He said it was a bargain, 'in the truest sense of the word', and that a jury conviction would likely have meant a much harsher sentence.
And Nodier's own lawyer said that, under the parole rules from 1985, he could expect to serve less than five years.

shots.label: Expected time served, his lawyer said

lines.say: Sheriff James Pohlmann said he would have liked to see him spend the rest of his life in prison.

shots.text: I would have liked to see him spend the rest of his life in prison.
shots.who: Sheriff James Pohlmann, St. Bernard Parish

lines.say: And John Doran, the detective who'd reopened the case, said: "Some form of justice has been served. Ten years is better than none."

shots.text: Some form of justice has been served. Ten years is better than none.
shots.who: John Doran, St. Bernard Parish Sheriff's Office

lines.say: On the eleventh of October, 2026, HBO premiered a three-part series about the case: The Pet Cemetery Murders: A Ghost Story.
It's a Lightbox production, written and directed by Philip Cairney. Parts two and three air on the eighteenth and twenty-fifth of October.
Its title says 'murders'. The legal record says manslaughter.
One critic, at RogerEbert.com, found the case itself thin, and said the series centres people who earnestly believe a woman's ghost helped solve her murder.

shots.label: ILLUSTRATION · GENERIC PET CEMETERY, NOT THE REAL SITE

rows.text: a thin case, told through believers

lines.say: No DNA breakthrough was ever reported here. The case was built on what witnesses said.
And Brandon Nodier today? Biography.com reports that his exact whereabouts are unknown. We found no public record of his release.
So, here's where the record stands.

shots.label: ILLUSTRATION · GENERIC PET CEMETERY, NOT THE REAL SITE

lines.say: Dorothy Thompson was sixty-one, and fighting in court for her land, when she disappeared.
Brandon Nodier, her groundskeeper, pleaded guilty to manslaughter in 2014, twenty-nine years after her death. He was sentenced to ten years.
Two witnesses said her ghost haunted them. Whatever you believe about that, what ended this case was a witness who said he was there, and a guilty plea.
